extracted.intended_audience: business communication students and instructors (people studying crisis communication for public figures/performers)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and instructional criteria for how public figures—particularly performers/comedians—should respond to public criticism and fact-checking, balancing integrity, evidence, tone, and reputation management. Emphasizes decisions about addressing allegations, presenting evidence, apologizing, and organizing the response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of truthfulness / integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: How much embellishment is acceptable — the line between 'emotional truth' and fabrication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted formulation: 'Every story in my style is built around a seed of truth... my comedy Arnold Palmer is seventy per cent emotional truth—this happened—and then thirty per cent hyperbole, exaggeration, fiction.' Students should discuss how much is too much 'stretching the truth' and whether embellishment undermines integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual norms of the medium (performative conventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the norms of comedy/performance allow greater use of hyperbole and fictionalized detail compared with other domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article contrasts comedians' use of dramatic effect with politicians or job applicants; guidance: recognize that medium matters and that audiences and critics may apply different standards (comedic license vs. factual reporting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role-specific standards of integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards of truth and ethical expectations differ across roles (comedians, politicians, organizational leaders, entrepreneurs, job applicants, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt for discussion: How might standards of integrity differ for comedians versus politicians or leaders? Consider moral standing arguments (e.g., claiming 'societal value' to justify embellishment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis response timing and strategy (address vs. move on)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to ignore criticism and move on, or address it directly — timing and extent of response matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical crisis management advises 'move on, not fixate.' But in an attention economy it can be strategic to address a controversy ('never let a good crisis go to waste'). Minhaj 'split the difference' — he didn't linger but dedicated a solid chunk of jokes to it, yielding large audience response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide evidence and transparent rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply corroborating evidence (audio, headlines, clips) and clearly distinguish between verified facts and artistic changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minhaj played audio from an interview, showed headlines and a Bill Maher clip, and 'distinguished between what really happened and how he changed details to create a funny/poignant story.' Good crisis responses should present supporting evidence and point out reporter omissions where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge harm and apologize where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and apologize to those hurt by one's routines or statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minhaj 'apologized to those hurt by his routines' while also defending his craft; effective responses often include explicit apologies to affected parties alongside explanatory context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear organization and message structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize the response with a clear main point up front and a conclusion that reiterates perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbatim note from piece: 'direct organization plan—up front!' Minhaj concluded with a main point (he didn't 'fake racism'). Presenting the main claim early helps audience comprehension and persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish core factual falsity from embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Make an ethical and factual distinction between fabrications that change the core truth of events and embellishments used for dramatic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minhaj emphasized he 'didn't “fake racism.”' Guidance: clarify whether changes alter the fundamental facts or merely dramatize them; this affects moral and reputational consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone sensitivity and avoiding trivialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful not to minimize or trivialize serious issues when responding (avoid joking about more serious scandals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example to avoid: Minhaj's quip that it was too bad the scandal wasn't about child abuse (an attempt at deflection that risks appearing insensitive). Responses should calibrate tone to avoid alienating audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use criticism strategically for reputational advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether highlighting criticism can convert a scandal into increased attention or a positive reputation shift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New York Times summary: by highlighting rather than downplaying criticism, Minhaj may have avoided being 'cancelled' and might even elevate his reputation; students should weigh risks and potential upside of leveraging controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for third-party fact-checking and media narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate fact-checking and independent reporting; prepare documentation and anticipate what reporters may confirm or dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malone's inability to confirm some stories prompted scrutiny; Minhaj's inclusion of recording evidence aimed to counter that. Guidance: expect independent analyses (e.g., Slate deep dives) and craft responses that address likely lines of inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure effectiveness by audience reaction and engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate response impact via audience reaction, social media engagement, and view counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators: Minhaj's dedicated jokes 'got one of the biggest responses of the night' and his 21-minute video had ~1.9 million views; use such metrics to judge whether the chosen strategy resonated.
